issues.explanation: The skill description frames the capability primarily as website/file publishing, but the body also includes private Drive storage operations, reading/writing stored files, and token-based sharing flows. Undeclared data-storage and sharing behaviors are security-relevant because they expand what user data may be transmitted, persisted, or exposed beyond the advertised purpose.
issues.remediation: Update the top-level metadata and description to fully disclose Drive functionality, token sharing, file read/write/delete operations, and any other storage features. Separate publishing and Drive management into distinct skills if possible so invocation scope matches user intent.

evidence.actual_behavior_summary: The supplied code is a CLI for here.now Drive storage management: creating/listing/deleting drives, uploading/downloading/importing/exporting files, reading file contents, deleting files, and creating/revoking drive sharing tokens with read/write permissions. It interacts with /api/v1/drives and direct object-storage upload URLs, not site publishing or domain-management endpoints.

evidence.actual_behavior_summary: A shell script that publishes local files/directories or Drive snapshots to here.now via its API, supports authenticated or anonymous publishes, workspace ownership, folders, TTL expiry, SPA/cross-origin-isolation flags, slug updates, claim tokens, and optimistic concurrency/version tracking. It uploads files to storage and finalizes the site publish.

issues.explanation: The skill exposes folder rename/delete endpoints and automatic folder creation from free-form names, which are account-mutating operations. In a broad-trigger skill, such write/delete capabilities can be abused or invoked unintentionally, causing organizational damage or data-management changes the user did not request.
issues.remediation: Restrict destructive or mutating folder operations behind explicit confirmation and narrow intent matching. Validate folder identifiers carefully, disable delete/rename unless the user clearly requests them, and separate organizational actions from simple publishing flows.
issues.code_snippet:
`--folder` takes a folder name or id. A name is matched case-insensitively and **created if it does not exist yet**, so this works the first time; the script reports the result as `publish_result.folder`. It requires an API key (anonymous Sites have no account to file in) and works with `--slug` (moves an existing Site) and `--workspace` (the workspace's folders).

Without the script, the same field is `folder` on `POST /api/v1/publish`, `PUT /api/v1/publish/{slug}`, and `PATCH /api/v1/publish/{slug}/metadata` (the way to file a Site without publishing a new version; `"folder": null` moves it back to the root). `GET /api/v1/folders` lists the account's folders; `GET /api/v1/publishes?folder={name-or-id}` lists one folder's Sites. Rename and delete are `PATCH`/`DELETE /api/v1/folders/{id}` (deleting a folder unfiles its Sites and deletes nothing else). Up to 50 folders per account, names up to 60 characters.

**Never invent folders or file Sites the user did not ask to file.** The folder structure is theirs; every folder appears as a tile in their dashboard. See https://here.now/docs#folders.

issues.explanation: The skill clearly instructs use of network access (`curl`, API calls) and shell execution (`./scripts/publish.sh`, file writes), but it declares no explicit tool scope or permissions boundary. That increases the chance an agent platform grants broader capabilities than the user expects, making unintended external transmission or local state changes easier.
issues.remediation: Add an explicit permissions/allowed-tools section declaring the minimum required capabilities (for example, scoped network access to `https://here.now` and storage endpoints plus specific local shell/file operations). Document which actions mutate local files, use credentials, or contact external services so the host can enforce least privilege.

issues.explanation: The trigger phrases are broad (`publish this`, `share this`, `generate a URL`, `build a chatbot`) and overlap with ordinary requests that may not imply consent to upload data to an external service. That can cause unintended invocation and accidental exfiltration of user content to a public or semi-public hosting platform.
issues.remediation: Narrow trigger phrases to explicit here.now/web-hosting intent and require confirmation before uploading or publishing any content externally. Add safeguards that verify visibility settings, destination account/workspace, and whether the user actually wants internet-accessible hosting.

issues.explanation: The install command uses `npx skills add heredotnow/skill --skill here-now -g` without pinning a version or digest. This creates a supply-chain risk: future upstream changes or a compromised package/version could alter the installed skill behavior unexpectedly.
issues.remediation: Pin the exact package version or commit SHA in installation instructions, and preferably provide integrity-verifiable release artifacts. Encourage upgrades through explicit reviewed version bumps rather than unbounded latest installs.

issues.explanation: This second unpinned `npx skills` reference carries the same supply-chain exposure as the first: installs may resolve to whatever package version is current at execution time. That undermines reproducibility and trust in reviewed behavior.
issues.remediation: Use a fully pinned package version or immutable source reference here as well. Keep all installation/update examples consistent so users are not steered toward unreviewed latest versions.

issues.explanation: Skill enables autonomous high-impact decisions without human-in-the-loop verification. Critical operations (destructive commands, financial transactions, data deletion) should require explicit user confirmation.
issues.remediation: Add human-in-the-loop confirmation for destructive, irreversible, or high-impact operations. Never auto-execute commands that modify files, send data, or alter system state.
issues.code_snippet:
Authenticated updates require a saved API key.

**Stale-base protection.** The live Site may have changed since your local files were published — the owner can edit it from other tools (another agent, the here.now Editor, a teammate). The script records the live `versionId` in `.herenow/state.json` after each publish and sends it as `baseVersionId` on the next update of the same slug from the same directory; if the live Site moved past it, the update is rejected with `code: "version_conflict"` naming the live version and what created it. When that happens, relay the message to the user and offer to (a) read the live files with `GET /api/v1/publish/{slug}/files` (lists them with a `url` each) and `GET /api/v1/publish/{slug}/files/{path}` (the bytes; owner API key, works for password-protected and restricted Sites without the visitor password), reconcile them into the local files, and republish, or (b) re-run with `--overwrite` to replace the live version anyway. Before editing local files for an authenticated Site you haven't touched recently, check for drift first: `GET /api/v1/publish/{slug}` returns `currentVersionId` plus `currentVersionSource` and `currentVersionCreatedAt` (what changed it and when, e.g. `editor`) — if the id differs from your state file's `versionId`, read the live files before editing. The published version is the shared truth; never fetch the public URL to read an owned Site (it is gated for protected Sites) and never ask the user for a visitor password to read their own Site. Anonymous Sites can't call these endpoints; they rely on the saved state and server enforcement. Omitting `baseVersionId` (or using `--overwrite`) is an unchecked full replacement — today's default for raw API callers.

Every publish records an immutable version. If the user asks to see earlier versions of a Site, undo a publish, or roll back: list history with `GET /api/v1/publish/{slug}/versions` and restore instantly with `POST /api/v1/publish/{slug}/versions/{versionId}/restore` (restoring keeps the current access mode, password, and domains). Version access is included on every plan, personal and workspace alike. A byte-identical republish returns `unchanged: true` from finalize instead of creating a new version. See https://here.now/docs#versions.

issues.explanation: The code uploads arbitrary local file contents directly to an externally supplied upload URL on cloud storage. Although this is part of normal publish/import behavior, in an agent context it is dangerous because local files selected by the agent can be exfiltrated off-host to a third-party storage endpoint, and the endpoint host differs from the primary service domain.
issues.remediation: Constrain which local paths the agent may upload, require explicit user consent before transmitting local files, and validate that upload URLs are restricted to an expected allowlist of storage domains. Add clear auditing of uploaded filenames/paths and optionally a dry-run/approval step before any external file transfer.

In an agent setting, this is sensitive because a prompt asking to 'share files' could be translated into creation of broadly scoped write-capable credentials, leading to unauthorized data tampering, deletion, or further token proliferation.
issues.remediation: Restrict the share command to read-only tokens by default and require an explicit high-trust confirmation flow for write or manage-token scopes. issues.explanation: The script performs direct network uploads of local file contents using curl PUT requests, which transmits user-selected local data to remote upload URLs. While the script logs progress like 'uploading ... files', it does not clearly disclose that local file contents are being sent off-host or warn about the privacy/integrity impact within the code comments, prompts, or visible user-facing warning text.
issues.remediation: Add an explicit user-facing disclosure before upload begins, such as printing that selected local files will be transmitted to remote storage/service endpoints. If appropriate, require a confirmation flag or interactive confirmation for first-time or sensitive publishes.

issues.explanation: The script blindly POSTs to FINALIZE_URL returned by the previous server response, reusing bearer auth and workspace headers without validating that the URL remains on the expected here.now origin. If a malicious or compromised API endpoint returned an attacker-controlled finalize URL, this could leak the API key and associated account-scoping headers to an arbitrary host.
issues.remediation: Before calling the finalize URL, parse and validate it against an allowlist of expected HTTPS origins/hosts, or ignore the full URL and construct the finalize endpoint locally from trusted response identifiers. Do not forward Authorization headers to untrusted or cross-origin finalize URLs.
